title: School choices on GCSE maths tier of entry
official: An evaluation of how school choices on examination tier impact pupil attainment in GCSE maths
summary:
Background and study aims
GCSE mathematics is an important qualification for young people in England. A grade 4 or above is usually needed to progress to many further education courses, apprenticeships and training programmes. GCSE mathematics can be taken at either foundation tier or higher tier. Pupils entered for the foundation tier can achieve grades 1 to 5, while pupils entered for the higher tier can achieve grades 4 to 9, although those who do not reach the required mark may receive a lower grade or no grade.
Current guidance recommends that pupils predicted to achieve a grade 5 should normally be entered for the foundation tier examination. However, some schools choose to enter these pupils for the higher tier examination instead. This study aims to find out how this decision affects pupils’ final GCSE mathematics results.

Who can participate?
Pupils aged 15 to 16 years who are:
1.	In Year 11 during the 2026/27 school year
2.	Taking GCSE mathematics in summer 2027 for the first time
3.	Predicted to achieve grade 5 in GCSE mathematics
4.	Attending a mainstream state-funded school in England

What does the study involve?
The study will compare GCSE mathematics results between pupils predicted to achieve grade 5 who are entered for the higher tier examination and similar pupils who are entered for the foundation tier examination.
Researchers will analyse GCSE examination results from around 4,200 pupils across approximately 140 schools. The study will also explore how schools make decisions about examination tier entry. This will include surveys of mathematics subject leaders and case studies in some schools. In selected schools, pupils may be invited to complete a survey about their experiences.
The study does not require pupils to receive any additional teaching programme or intervention beyond their normal education. Schools will continue to make examination entry decisions as they usually would.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
The study may help schools, teachers and policy makers better understand whether entering pupils predicted to achieve grade 5 for the higher tier mathematics examination affects their academic achievement. The findings could help improve future decisions about GCSE mathematics examination entry.
The risks to participants are expected to be low, as the study mainly involves the analysis of educational data and surveys. Some pupils may be asked to complete a questionnaire, but participation is not expected to involve any significant burden or harm.

Where is the study run from?
The study is run from Sheffield Hallam University, Sheffield, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
November 2026 to July 2027.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF).

Who is the main contact?
Dr Martin Culliney
M.Culliney@shu.ac.uk

interventions.name: The Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation (Ofqual), the body that regulates assessments and examinations in England, recommends that pupils predicted to achieve grade 5 at GCSE should be entered for the foundation tier examination. Some  schools enter these pupils into the higher tier

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Pupils taking GCSE maths in summer 2027 at mainstream, state-funded schools in England who are predicted a grade 5 in that subject.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Pupils not in Year 11 for 2026/27 school year
2. Pupils not predicted grade 5 in GCSE maths
3. Pupils in non-mainstream or non-state funded schools
